opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is moving from a team where everyone does everything to one where people own specific areas and trust each other to deliver.

Early on, a startup is basically a group of people sitting around one table. Information moves instantly, decisions happen in a hallway conversation, and if something breaks, whoever notices it just fixes it. That's a huge advantage at the beginning. You move very fast because there's almost no coordination cost.

But that model doesn't scale. Once you go from ten people to thirty or fifty, the founders can't be in every conversation, and you start to see things fall through the cracks. Two people solve the same problem, or nobody solves it because everyone assumes someone else will. So the first transition is defining ownership: who is responsible for this system, this customer, this decision. It doesn't have to be heavy process. It just has to be clear.

The second thing, which I think is harder for technical founders, is learning to let go. When you've built something with your own hands, it's tempting to keep reviewing every pull request and making every architecture call. At some point that turns you into the bottleneck. Your job changes from being the best individual contributor to building a team that can make good decisions without you, and that means hiring people who are better than you in their areas and actually giving them authority.

Third, you have to be deliberate about culture and communication, because the things that happened naturally when you were small now need some structure. Why are we doing this? What's the priority this quarter? What does good work look like here? When you're small everyone absorbs that through osmosis. When you're bigger you need to write it down, repeat it, and make sure new people get the same context the early team had.

And the last point is that I don't think there's one moment where you "become" a big company. It's continuous. The structure that works at twenty people will feel wrong at sixty, and again at two hundred. So I think a healthy organization is one that's willing to keep revisiting how it works, and to keep the speed and ownership mindset of the early days while adding just enough structure to stay coordinated. Too little process and you get chaos. Too much and you lose what made you a startup. Most of the work is finding that balance over and over again.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving beyond a model where everyone handles everything and founders make every decision, toward clear ownership, delegated authority, and enough organizational structure to coordinate the team.

r002.rationale: It says culture and communication need deliberate structure as the company grows, and that the organization must keep revisiting how it works.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it as a few distinct phases, and the mistake people make is trying to skip one.

In the very beginning, you don't really have an organization. You have a handful of people who all know everything. There's no process, there's barely any communication overhead, and that's the point. At LMSYS and in the early days of SGLang, we were a small group of researchers and engineers who could basically read each other's minds. Decisions happened in a chat thread or over lunch. If you try to impose structure at that stage, you just slow yourself down.

The first real transition comes when you cross maybe fifteen or twenty people. Suddenly not everyone can hold the whole picture in their head anymore. That's when you need to start writing things down, having clear owners for each area, and being deliberate about who makes which decisions. For us, open source actually forced that discipline early, because the community needed to understand the codebase and the roadmap without being in the room. Writing good design docs and public RFCs turned out to be a forcing function for internal clarity too.

The second transition is harder, and it's about the founders themselves. Early on, the founders are the best individual contributors. They write the hardest code, they close the key relationships. At some point the company outgrows that, and the founders have to shift from doing to enabling. That's painful, because the thing that made you good is now the thing you need to stop doing. You have to hire people who are better than you at specific things and then actually let them own it.

The third piece I'd highlight is culture. In the early days culture is just who you are. As you scale, you have to make it explicit, because new people didn't live through the founding moments. What do we value? How do we handle disagreement? How much do we prioritize performance versus shipping quickly? If you don't articulate that, every new hire fills in the blanks with wherever they came from, and after a year you have five different cultures under one roof.

The last thing I'd say is that you shouldn't over-plan this. Every stage has its own problems, and the structure that works at fifty people will break at two hundred. So the goal isn't to find the perfect org chart. It's to build a team that can notice when things are breaking and change quickly, without too much ego attached to how things used to work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts an early team that relies on everyone knowing everything with later needs for documented processes, clear ownership, and defined decision-making.

r002.rationale: It describes several distinct transitions and says teams must deliberately establish structure and make culture explicit as they grow.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest transition is from relying on a few people who know everything to building an organization where people can make good decisions without knowing everything.

Early on, coordination happens naturally. You’re sitting together, everyone talks to the founders, and if something changes, the whole team knows. As you grow, that stops working. If every decision still has to go through the same two or three people, they become the bottleneck.

So you need to make things explicit: What are our priorities? Who owns a decision? What can a team decide independently, and when should it involve other teams? That sounds like adding process, but done well, it actually gives people more freedom.

There’s also a personal transition for the founders. Being involved in every detail can feel like you’re maintaining quality. But eventually your job is to create the context, hire people you trust, and let them take responsibility. You have to accept that they may do things differently from you.

The tricky part is timing. You don’t want to build a big-company structure before you need it. But you also can’t assume that what worked for ten people will work for a hundred. I’d look for repeated problems—decisions getting stuck, work being duplicated, priorities being interpreted differently—and introduce enough structure to address those problems.

r001.rationale: It describes moving from reliance on a few people to an organization where teams can decide independently, supported by explicit priorities, ownership, and processes.

r002.rationale: It says the transition requires intentionally making decisions and responsibilities explicit and adding structure in response to recurring problems; it does not happen automatically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest transition is from relying on individual people to building an organization that can operate without the founders being involved in every decision. Early on, everyone has context. You sit together, you talk constantly, and you can change direction very quickly. As the company grows, that shared context stops happening automatically.

So you have to become much more deliberate about what the priorities are, who owns which decisions, and how information travels. That doesn’t mean adding process everywhere. It means asking, “What do people need to know so they can make good decisions independently?”

There’s also a personal transition for the founders. The things that made you effective early—being involved in everything, solving problems yourself—can eventually become bottlenecks. You have to move from doing the work to creating the conditions for other people to do it well. And that requires giving people real ownership, including room to approach a problem differently than you would.

r001.rationale: It describes moving from reliance on individuals and founder involvement to an organization that can operate independently, supported by clear priorities, decision ownership, and information flow.

r002.rationale: It says shared context stops happening automatically as the company grows and that leaders must deliberately define priorities, decision ownership, and how information travels.
